lead: Shannon proved codes can come close to capacity. BCH codes are cyclic codes with a guaranteed minimum distance. Turbo codes run two convolutional encoders in parallel, split by an interleaver, and decode by passing soft messages. LDPC codes do the same on a sparse graph. Turbo and LDPC reach within about a decibel of capacity; BCH stays a few dB away. Wi-Fi, 4G/5G data links and flash controllers run these codes.
prereq: You need: 7.5 for the capacity wall, 7.6 for d_min and the Hamming bound, 7.7 for generator polynomials, and 7.8 for trellis and soft decisions.

sections.h3: BCH codes: a guaranteed number of errors

blocks.text: BCH stands for Bose–Chaudhuri–Hocquenghem. A BCH code is a cyclic code (see 7.7) whose generator polynomial g(x) is built around a chosen error count t. Pick t first; the code then corrects any t errors in the block.

The arithmetic runs in GF(2<sup>m</sup>), a field with 2<sup>m</sup> elements, formed by adjoining to GF(2) a root α of a primitive polynomial. A binary BCH code contains every polynomial over GF(2) that has α, α², …, α<sup>2t</sup> as roots. Those 2t consecutive powers create the distance guarantee.
n = 2<sup>m</sup> − 1,   d<sub>min</sub> ≥ 2t + 1,   k = n − deg g(x),   R = k/n
blocks.where: n is the block length in bits, m is the field exponent, t is the number of correctable errors, d_min is the minimum Hamming distance, g(x) is the generator polynomial, k is the number of message bits and R is the code rate.

blocks.text: Take m = 4, so n = 15. Two common codes are the (15,7) code with t = 2 and d_min ≥ 5, and the (15,5) code with t = 3 and d_min ≥ 7. The (15,7) code sends 7 message bits in 15, so R = 0.467.

Decoding works on polynomials: the syndromes give an error-locator polynomial, its roots give the error positions, and those bits are flipped. Berlekamp–Massey finds the locator; a Chien search finds its roots.
Reed–Solomon codes use the same construction on symbols of GF(2<sup>m</sup>) instead of single bits. They fight bursts well and appear on CDs, DVDs, QR codes and deep-space links.

sections.h3: Turbo codes: two encoders, one interleaver

blocks.text: A turbo code makes two encoders read the same block in different orders, then lets two decoders exchange soft opinions about every bit.

Encoding: block d enters a recursive systematic convolutional (RSC) encoder, which sends d out unchanged — systematic — and adds parity p1. The interleaver π, a fixed permutation, shuffles d into a second RSC encoder producing p2. A multiplexer sends d, p1 and p2: three output bits per input bit, R = 1/3.

Recursive means the shift register has feedback, so its state depends on a running sum of past inputs. A single 1 does not quickly return the trellis to the all-zero state, which removes most low-weight codewords.
Puncturing raises the rate by deleting parity bits. Drop half of p1 and half of p2 and each input bit sends 1 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2 bits, so R = 1/2.

The interleaver is the heart of the design. A pattern giving a low-weight codeword in encoder 1 is scattered into high-weight data for encoder 2, so a low-weight codeword needs both encoders to agree, which is rare.

Decoding is iterative and soft. Decoder 1 takes the systematic bits and p1, computes a reliability (log-likelihood ratio) per bit, removes what it already knew, and passes the leftover extrinsic information to decoder 2 along with p2. Decoder 2 answers the same way. A few rounds suffice. Each decoder is a MAP (BCJR) detector or the simpler SOVA. On blocks of thousands of bits, turbo codes come within about a decibel of capacity. LTE uses them for data channels.

sections.h3: LDPC codes: belief propagation on a sparse graph

blocks.text: An LDPC (low-density parity-check) code is a linear block code (see 7.6) whose parity-check matrix H is sparse: almost every entry is zero, with few 1s in each row and column. Sparsity lets n reach thousands of bits and still decode in real time.

The code is drawn as a Tanner graph with two kinds of nodes. Each variable node is one of the n code bits and holds a soft belief about it. Each check node is one parity equation, that is, one row of H, and there are n − k of them. An edge joins variable v to check c wherever H has a 1.

Decoding is belief propagation. Each round, every variable node sends its belief along its edges. Each check node combines the beliefs it receives and replies with how strongly each bit is constrained by its parity equation. Variable nodes then update. Only the 1s of H are touched, so a round costs time proportional to the number of edges, not to n².

Regular (j,k) codes have j ones per column and k ones per row; irregular codes with mixed degrees do better. Long blocks with good degree distributions come within a fraction of a decibel of capacity. Short blocks or badly chosen degrees show an error floor: the bit error rate curve flattens at high SNR instead of falling steeply. Wi-Fi (802.11n/ac), DVB-S2 satellite television and 5G data channels use LDPC.

All three are linear codes. They differ in block length, decoder and cost. Longer blocks with soft iterative decoding buy closeness to capacity; the price is latency, since the whole block must be buffered, and decoder complexity.
One rule holds throughout: no code beats capacity (7.5). A code changes how close you get to the wall, never where the wall stands.

examples.question: A link is offered a BCH (15,7) code and a turbo code. (a) For the BCH code find n, k, t, d_min, R, and check the Hamming bound. (b) The turbo encoder uses two rate-1/2 RSC encoders and sends the systematic bit with both parity bits; find the rate, then the rate after puncturing every second parity bit.
steps: Read n = 15 and k = 7 from the notation (n,k).
The block length fixes m: n = 2^m − 1 = 15 gives m = 4. For m = 4 the (15,7) BCH code has t = 2.
Hamming bound check. Patterns of weight ≤ 2: 1 + C(15,1) + C(15,2) = 1 + 15 + 105 = 121.
The bound requires 2^k × 121 ≤ 2^n, i.e. 121 ≤ 2^(15−7) = 256. It holds, with 135 to spare.
Spare room does not make it a 3-error code: correcting 3 would need 1 + 15 + 105 + 455 = 576 ≤ 256, which fails.
Turbo, mother code: output per input bit is 1 systematic + 1 + 1 parity = 3, so R = 1/3 = 0.3333.
Puncturing every second parity bit keeps half of p1 and half of p2. Output per input bit = 1 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2, so R = 1/2 = 0.5.
examples.answer: The (15,7) BCH code has n = 15, k = 7, t = 2, d_min ≥ 5, R = 0.4667, and satisfies the Hamming bound since 121 ≤ 256. The turbo code has mother rate 1/3 = 0.3333 and punctured rate 1/2 = 0.5.
examples.check:
n = 15
k = 7
t = 2
dmin = 2*t + 1
R = round(k/n, 4)
patterns2 = 1 + n + n*(n-1)//2
bound = 2**(n-k)
patterns3 = patterns2 + n*(n-1)*(n-2)//6
R3 = round(1/3, 4)
Rhalf = 2/3 - 1/6  # 1 + 0.5 + 0.5 bits per input bit -> 1/2
print(n)
print(k)
print(t)
print(dmin)
print(R)
print(patterns2)
print(bound)
print(patterns3)
print(R3)
print(Rhalf)

traps: Thinking a strong code can beat capacity. Turbo and LDPC codes approach the Shannon limit from below; nothing works above it.
Confusing code rate with redundancy when puncturing is given. Recount the bits actually transmitted, not the mother code's bits.
Writing d_min = 2t + 1 as exact. The design guarantees d_min ≥ 2t + 1; the true minimum distance may be larger.
Using n = 2^m − 1 with the wrong m. n = 15 needs m = 4, not m = 15.
Making the turbo rate 1/4. The systematic bit goes out once, so two rate-1/2 encoders make 1/3, not 1/4.

quiz.q: Expand BCH and state what t means in a t-error-correcting BCH code.
quiz.a: Bose–Chaudhuri–Hocquenghem. t is the number of bit errors the code is designed to correct; the code then has minimum distance at least 2t + 1.

quiz.q: In an LDPC code, what exactly is sparse, and how is the code drawn?
quiz.a: The parity-check matrix H is sparse, with very few 1s per row and column. It is drawn as a Tanner graph: variable nodes for code bits, check nodes for parity equations, one edge per 1 in H.

quiz.q: Why does the interleaver improve a turbo code?
quiz.a: A bit pattern giving a low-weight codeword in the first encoder becomes a high-weight pattern for the second. A low-weight codeword then needs both encoders to agree, which is rare.

quiz.q: Why must turbo and LDPC decoders work on soft values rather than decided bits?
quiz.a: The iterations exchange reliabilities, that is log-likelihood ratios. Deciding each bit to 0 or 1 throws away the confidence the next decoder needs, and most of the coding gain disappears.

quiz.q: A binary BCH code has n = 31 and t = 3. Find m, the guaranteed d_min, and the number of error patterns of weight ≤ 3.
For the (15,7) BCH code, 121 ≤ 2^8 = 256 satisfies the Hamming bound with 135 to spare. Does that spare room mean the code can correct 3 errors?
quiz.a: No. Correcting 3 errors needs 1 + 15 + 105 + 455 = 576 ≤ 256, which fails. The code is guaranteed only t = 2; the spare room does not upgrade it.

quiz.q: A flash memory controller and a 5G data channel both need forward error correction. Pick between BCH, turbo and LDPC for each, with one reason.
quiz.a: Flash: BCH, because its algebraic hard-decision decoder is simple and fast at the short block lengths used. 5G data: LDPC, because very long blocks with belief propagation come within a fraction of a decibel of capacity.

beyond: Not for the exam. 5G NR uses LDPC for shared data and polar codes for control information, both from the same soft message-passing family. Current research adds spatial coupling and probabilistic amplitude shaping to squeeze within a tenth of a decibel of capacity. Search for "Tanner graph", "sum-product algorithm", "5G NR LDPC base graph" and "polar codes" to go further.
